input:
In this worked example, the goal is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min has elapsed. The measured rate constant is k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min.

For a first-order reaction, the rate constant k fixes the half-life t1/2 through the relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, whilst the fraction remaining after time t can be expressed as exp(-k t). It is important to emphasise that these relations are valid for a first-order reaction only, since a reaction of any other order would follow an entirely different decay law, meaning that neither relation could simply be transferred across.

Substituting k = 0.046 min-1 into the half-life relation gives t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.046 = 15.1 min. The half-life can be understood as the time taken for the concentration to drop to exactly one half of its value at the start of the interval, and it is worth noting that t1/2 does not depend on the starting concentration, so every interval of 15.1 min halves whatever amount remains at its start. Substituting t = 60 min into the decay relation gives the fraction remaining as exp(-0.046 x 60) = 0.06. Reassuringly, the two results are fully consistent, because 60 min spans several half-lives of 15.1 min, and repeated halving over such a span naturally leaves only a very small fraction of the reactant, which is precisely what the value 0.06 indicates. Overall, the half-life of 15.1 min effectively sets the timescale of the reaction at 323 K, meaning that measurements intended to follow the decay need to be spaced well inside a single half-life, just as the stated readings every 5 min over 90 min indeed are.

The two relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither relation transfers to it.

Substitution of k = 0.046 min-1 gives t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.046 = 15.1 min. The half-life is the time in which the concentration falls to one half of its value at the start of the interval, and t1/2 does not depend on the starting concentration: every interval of 15.1 min halves the amount that remains at its start. Substitution of t = 60 min gives the fraction remaining as exp(-0.046 x 60) = 0.06. The two results agree with each other: 60 min spans several half-lives of 15.1 min, and repeated halving over that span leaves only a small fraction of the reactant, which is what the value 0.06 states.
